title: Reading the Floor
passage:
At half past six the indoor school is lit, empty and cold, and the tractor is already in it, towing a leveller down the long side. What it is levelling is not soil. The floor is 130 millimetres of washed silica sand, mixed through with chopped fibre and coated in wax, laid over a membrane and crushed stone. It went down nine years ago. For two winters the riders here have been saying that the school changes under them: hard and slippery for a January lesson, deep and tiring by a July afternoon. The yard has blamed the machine, then the mix, then the man on the tractor.

Mervyn Pallenmoor tests riding surfaces for an insurer that covers about four hundred yards. He came in February with a drop tester in the boot: a weighted steel foot on a rail, released from a fixed height, with an accelerometer bolted inside it. It reports two numbers – how sharply the surface stops the foot, and how far the foot slides before it stops. He read a grid at seven, with the school at three degrees, and the same grid again at four, with it at eighteen. Both numbers moved, and they moved together: in the cold the foot stopped dead in two-thirds of the distance the warm floor needed, and slid less doing so. He has been back four times since, in July as well as in January. He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas, some of them older than this one. In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre and kept damp with a sprinkler, the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another. The waxed ones move, whatever their age. “The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is,” Pallenmoor says. “A number for it is more than these readings will carry; the blend under the sand isn’t the same from one supplier to the next. The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test.”

The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work. Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together, and a hoof breaks the surface rather than pushing it aside. Above about twenty-five it goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep. Then there is the machine, though not in the way the yard meant it. The leveller’s tines were set to 50 millimetres. The bed is 130. Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on. Pallenmoor cored the bed in eleven places. In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3. Harrowing lifts fibre, and fibre is what keeps sand from packing, so the machine had been slowly sorting the bed into a loose layer riding on a hard one. The sand itself had hardly changed: the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them, and the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top.

What the yard wants to know is whether any of this keeps a horse sound. Here Pallenmoor is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him. The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above his steel foot. He has readings from a hundred and forty arenas and injury records he would trust from hardly any of them: the yards with good records are the ones that do everything else well. The one association he will argue for is not with any surface but with change – a horse schooled on one footing and jumped on another – and he says he would argue it from the veterinary literature rather than from his own figures. That is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are.

The yard has changed two things and left the rest alone. A timer brings the heaters on at five, to have the school above eight degrees before the first lesson; the bill is real, and the yard has decided it is worth paying. The tines have been dropped to 80 millimetres, with a length of angle iron welded across the frame so that nobody has to set them by eye, and for a month the tractor went over twice a day to bring the pan up. At ten past seven on a February morning the tine marks run the length of the school in even rows, and the thermometer screwed to the post by the gate reads nine.
– Bridget Tullis

questions.prompt: What is said about Pallenmoor’s readings inside the school?

options.text: He recorded how sharply the foot stopped, but not how far it slid.
The foot was released by hand, so the drop varied from one reading to the next.
In the cold the same drop stopped the foot in a shorter distance and slid less.
The difference between one arena and the next is wider than the difference between his visits.

questions.rationale:
C is right. The same foot, dropped the same way, behaved differently at the two temperatures: “in the cold the foot stopped dead in two-thirds of the distance the warm floor needed, and slid less doing so”. Both of the tester’s numbers moved, and both moved the same way.

A takes half the instrument away. The passage sets out what it does: “It reports two numbers – how sharply the surface stops the foot, and how far the foot slides before it stops”. The slide is one of the two things recorded, not something the tester leaves out.

B offers a reason for the cold reading that the method rules out. The foot is “released from a fixed height”, which is the one thing a drop tester cannot be allowed to vary; a reader who wants the difference explained away as sloppy work will reach for this.

D turns the comparison in the quotation the other way up. What Pallenmoor says is that “The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test”: the seasons separate his readings by more than the arenas do, not by less.

questions.prompt: What was shown by the cores Pallenmoor took from the bed?

options.text: The wax had worn off the grains in the lower part of the bed.
The sand had broken down into finer grains than the specification called for.
Below the tines the bed had stayed loose, since no hoof ever reaches that deep.
There was much less fibre in the bottom of the bed than in the top.

questions.rationale:
D is right. Pallenmoor “cored the bed in eleven places”, and the cores divide it in two: “In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3”. The fibre sits where the tines reach and thins out below them.

A moves a real finding to the wrong end of the bed. The wax was looked at, and what came up was the opposite: “the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top”.

B is the ageing story that a nine-year-old floor invites, and the sieve refuses it: “the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them”.

C reads like the sensible consequence of a machine that never reaches the bottom, and the passage says the reverse. The eighty millimetres the tines miss “had gone firm enough to lean a spade on”, packed by nine years of hoofprints rather than left loose by them.

questions.prompt: What is suggested about schools that are kept damp rather than waxed?

options.text: Their beds are newer than this one, so they have not begun to settle.
Having no wax in them is what leaves them riding much the same all day.
They carry no fibre, so there is nothing in them to stiffen when the school is cold.
They are read at a different hour, so the two grids never catch the change.

questions.rationale:
B is right. The damp schools differ from this one in a single respect the passage keeps in view: there is no wax on their sand. Their two grids “sit almost on top of one another”, while “The waxed ones move, whatever their age”. Take the coating away and the hour of the day stops mattering.

A reaches for age, which the passage has already closed off. The other arenas include “some of them older than this one”, and the waxed floors swing whatever age they are.

C swaps one ingredient for the other. Those schools are “laid on plain sand and fibre”, so fibre is exactly what they do have; the coating is what they have not.

D would explain the flat readings away as an artefact of timing. It cannot: he has “the same pair of grids” from every arena, the morning one and the afternoon one alike.

questions.prompt: How does the writer regard the idea that testing of this kind can show which arenas keep horses sound?

options.text: She takes the limits Pallenmoor sets on his own figures to be the honest ones.
She treats the tie between changing a horse’s footing and injury as settled by his readings.
She thinks work of this kind gives a yard nothing it can act on.
She is readier to doubt the riders’ account than to doubt his figures.

questions.rationale:
A is right. The writer gives her verdict in the paragraph itself. Pallenmoor “is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him”, and what he will not claim “is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are”. She backs the limit, not the promise.

B moves the expert one step past his own position and then hands that position to the writer. The single association he will argue for is the one about changing a horse’s footing, and he says he would argue it “from the veterinary literature rather than from his own figures”. Arguing from somebody else’s evidence is one thing; settling a question with your own figures is another.

C mistakes a limit for a dismissal. Nothing in the piece treats the testing as useless: the yard acts on it, drops its tines and puts its heaters on a timer.

D points the doubt at the wrong party, and sounds even-handed doing it. The riders said the school changed under them and the readings bore them out; it is the claim about soundness, not the complaint, that the writer holds at arm’s length.

questions.prompt: What can be concluded from this text?

options.text: The cold is probably doing damage to a bed that is near the end of its life.
A school that is kept warm will ride in February much as it rides in July.
The school’s temperature and the depth the tines reach are what settle how it rides.
The tractor’s work may matter more to the school than the temperature does.

questions.rationale:
C is right. Two things are shown to govern the floor and the yard has now set both: the temperature, which Pallenmoor says is “doing more in that room than the tractor is”, and the depth of the tines, which had been leaving eighty millimetres of the bed unturned since it was laid.

A blames age. The floor is nine years old, so the option is easy to believe, and the coring found the material sound: the grains as specified, and the wax at the bottom in better condition than the wax at the top.

B takes the winter half of the argument and drops the summer half. Warmth is not a cure in itself, because above about twenty-five degrees the coating “goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep”, which is the July complaint.

D reverses the weight the passage puts on the two. The sentence is a plain one: “The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is”. The tractor’s work counts, but it counts for less.

No contradictory dyad - B agrees with no option and contradicts none; A and D are on axes C does not touch. Two degradation claims (A wax, B sand), one state claim (C), one distribution claim (D, the key), so there is no 3+1 odd-one-out cluster and no dyad. Four different objects, not four points on one line: the expert's own caution (A), the status of one specific association (B), the value of the whole enterprise (C), the credibility of the riders (D). Two options are measured in tone (A and D) and two are strong (B and C), so 'pick the even-handed one' does not select the key. generator_meta.mechanism_verification_note: The physical claims are the ordinary behaviour of a waxed sand-and-fibre arena surface and are stated at the level the passage can support. Wax-coated silica sand with chopped synthetic fibre stiffens as the coating hardens in cold and loosens as it softens in heat; a watered, unwaxed sand-and-fibre bed does not have that coating and so does not swing with the room's temperature in the same way. Harrowing lifts fibre towards the top of the bed, and the layer below the tines consolidates under repeated hoof loading, which is why a shallow tine setting produces a loose layer riding on a firm one. The drop tester is described only by what it does - a weighted foot released from a fixed height, an accelerometer inside it, two outputs - and the readings are given as relative differences (two-thirds of the distance) rather than as absolute g figures, so no numerical claim is made that a specialist could check against a particular instrument. The temperatures are given as approximate ranges with 'about'. Nothing in the unit names a real product, blend, manufacturer or standard.
